paragraphs: This paper studies how to evaluate a policy using experience collected under another policy when the objective is long-run average reward. Evaluation requires estimating both the reward rate and the differential value function, which describes value relative to that ongoing reward rate. Function approximation makes these estimates possible without separately representing every state.

The difficulty is that this setting requires bootstrapping: updating estimates using other estimates. Together with off-policy data and function approximation, this creates the combination known as the deadly triad. The authors introduce two algorithms that extend the successful Gradient TD approach to the average-reward setting.

For linear function approximation, the paper establishes convergence for differential-value estimation. It also establishes convergence for reward-rate estimation without requiring a density-ratio estimate. These are distinct theoretical contributions, rather than a blanket guarantee for arbitrary neural networks. Experiments additionally examine nonlinear variants and report advantages over a competitive density-ratio-based method in both a simple domain and challenging robot simulations.
icml-2021-average-reward-off-policy-poli.tldr: Two algorithms provide convergent off-policy evaluation with linear function approximation for average reward, without density-ratio estimation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become unstable when it combines data from another policy, an approximate value function, and updates that rely on existing value estimates. This combination is called the deadly triad. The paper investigates whether target networks can provide a theoretically justified way to stabilize algorithms with all three ingredients.

The authors propose a target-network update that adds two projections to the commonly used Polyak-averaging update. They combine this mechanism with ridge regularization and apply it to several algorithms that otherwise diverge. Their analysis shows convergence to regularized temporal-difference fixed points, specifying what the stabilized learning process approaches.

The results cover linear function approximation across policy evaluation and control, including both discounted and average-reward objectives. A highlighted contribution is convergent linear Q-learning under nonrestrictive, changing behavior policies, without requiring bi-level optimization. The significance is theoretical support for a particular target-network construction combined with regularization; the stated results concern these analyzed algorithms and their regularized fixed points.
icml-2021-breaking-the-deadly-triad-with.tldr: A modified target-network update combined with ridge regularization makes several linear reinforcement-learning algorithms converge despite the deadly triad.

paragraphs: Giving a language model a few examples inside a prompt can produce strikingly uneven results. This paper shows that changing the prompt format, the examples, or even their order can move accuracy from near chance to near state-of-the-art. It connects this instability to preferences for particular answers, including answers appearing late in the prompt or frequently in pretraining data.

The proposed contextual calibration procedure measures these preferences before using the model on meaningful test inputs. It keeps the training prompt but supplies a content-free input such as N/A. The resulting answer probabilities reveal how strongly the prompt and model favor each answer without useful test content.

The authors then fit calibration parameters so that this content-free prediction becomes uniform across answers. Across diverse tasks, this adjustment substantially improves GPT-3 and GPT-2 accuracy and reduces sensitivity to prompt choices. The largest reported improvement is 30.0 percentage points. The finding shows that correcting contextual answer preferences can improve both performance and consistency in few-shot prompting.
icml-2021-calibrate-before-use-improving.tldr: Calibrating answer probabilities with a content-free input improves few-shot language-model accuracy and reduces sensitivity to prompt choices.

paragraphs: Training deep networks on large datasets can be computationally expensive. This paper aims to replace a large training set with a much smaller collection of synthetic images that still supports training a network from scratch. The goal is to preserve as much predictive performance as possible while reducing the amount of training data.

The proposed Differentiable Siamese Augmentation makes data augmentation useful during the construction of those synthetic images. This matters because the condensed set must carry useful training information even when networks are subsequently trained with augmentations. The method therefore connects how the images are synthesized with how they will be used for learning.

Experiments report substantial gains over prior methods, including 7% improvements on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. Using less than 1% of the data, the method achieves relative performance of 99.6% on MNIST, 94.9% on FashionMNIST, 88.5% on SVHN, and 71.5% on CIFAR10. These are relative-performance figures, not absolute accuracies. Applications to continual learning and architecture search also produce promising results.
icml-2021-dataset-condensation-with-diff.tldr: Differentiable Siamese Augmentation helps synthesize tiny training datasets that retain substantial predictive performance when used to train networks from scratch.

paragraphs: Continuous-control agents often explore by adding independent noise to each action or by perturbing policy parameters for an entire trajectory. These approaches organize randomness over different time spans. Earlier work found benefits from balancing them for linear policies, but that approach did not scale to policies represented by deep neural networks.

Deep coherent exploration provides a scalable framework that generalizes both step-based and trajectory-based exploration. It treats the parameters in the policy network’s last layer as latent variables. A recursive inference step within the policy update handles those variables, allowing the exploration mechanism to be incorporated into deep reinforcement learning.

The approach matters because the temporal structure of exploration becomes part of the learning framework, rather than being restricted to either independent action noise or a trajectory-wide perturbation. Experiments report faster and more stable learning for A2C, PPO, and SAC on several continuous-control tasks. These findings demonstrate benefits across the tested algorithms and tasks while keeping the contribution centered on exploration.
icml-2021-deep-coherent-exploration-for-.tldr: Deep coherent exploration unifies step-based and trajectory-based exploration and improves learning speed and stability on tested continuous-control tasks.

paragraphs: Quantizing a neural network requires choosing how many bits to use, which numerical range to represent, and the spacing between available values. These choices interact and can require extensive manual tuning. They are especially challenging for compact networks, where different layers may prefer different quantization settings.

Differentiable Dynamic Quantization, or DDQ, makes all of these choices learnable through a fully differentiable approach. Instead of treating precision, range, and step size as separately tuned settings, it learns them within the quantization method. This flexibility enables the approach to handle lightweight architectures such as MobileNets.

The resulting computation can use low-precision matrix-vector multiplication, making the method compatible with hardware including ARM. Experiments report improvements over previous approaches across multiple networks and benchmarks, particularly for already compact models. The highlighted result is lossless 4-bit quantization of MobileNetV2 on ImageNet, which the authors identify as a first. Here, lossless refers to the reported preservation of model performance under quantization.
icml-2021-differentiable-dynamic-quantiz.tldr: DDQ learns quantization precision, range, and spacing together, reporting lossless 4-bit quantization of MobileNetV2 on ImageNet.

paragraphs: Models that classify or match graphs can fail when an adversary makes small changes to graph connections or node attributes. Existing defenses often focus on a particular attack or task. This paper proposes ERNN, a graph-adaptive network intended to improve robustness across multiple-graph learning without tailoring the defense to a specific attack.

The design combines a Weibull activation function with constraints on the layer weights. At layer l, the activation enforces a gradient norm of K_l, while the weight norm is constrained to its reciprocal. Nearest matrix orthogonalization and polar decomposition impose the weight constraint while keeping the constrained weights close to their original values.

Together, these components produce a 1-Lipschitz network, controlling how strongly the network can amplify input changes while seeking to retain expressive power. The paper derives lower and upper bounds on feasible values of K_l under that constraint. Its central contribution is this coordinated activation-and-weight construction and its theoretical analysis for robust multiple-graph learning.
icml-2021-expressive-1-lipschitz-neural-.tldr: ERNN combines constrained weights and a Weibull activation to build expressive 1-Lipschitz networks for robust multiple-graph learning.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search must estimate which network designs perform well without spending too much computation evaluating them. Training every candidate separately is expensive. One-shot search reduces that expense by sharing weights inside a single supernetwork, but interactions among operations can make the resulting performance estimates inaccurate.

Few-shot NAS divides the search space among several smaller supernetworks. Each covers a different region, reducing the unwanted co-adaptation caused by placing every candidate in one shared network. The paper reports more accurate architecture evaluation than one-shot NAS, with only a small increase in evaluation cost.

Using up to seven sub-supernetworks, the method finds models reaching 80.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and 98.72% on CIFAR10; the latter uses neither extra data nor transfer learning. It also improves published Auto-GAN results by up to 20%. Broader experiments show improvements across four gradient-based and six search-based methods, supporting the usefulness of dividing weight sharing across multiple supernetworks rather than treating it as a single universal approximation.
icml-2021-few-shot-neural-architecture-s.tldr: Few-shot NAS improves architecture evaluation by distributing weight sharing across several supernetworks, with a small increase in evaluation cost.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, a joint policy describes how agents act together, while individual policies describe each agent’s behavior. Decomposed actor-critic methods try to connect these levels, but existing approaches discussed in the paper lack a guarantee of convergence to a global optimum. FOP addresses this gap through policy factorization.

The method starts from the optimal joint policy induced by a maximum-entropy multi-agent objective and factorizes it into individual policies. The authors prove that FOP’s factorized policies converge to the global optimum. This links the decomposition itself to the desired joint solution, rather than relying only on evidence that separately learned behaviors coordinate successfully.

Experiments in matrix and differential games verify convergence to global optima for both discrete and continuous action spaces. The authors also evaluate FOP on StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, where it substantially outperforms the compared state-of-the-art decomposed value-based and actor-critic methods. Together, the theory and experiments support factorization as a way to connect individual policies with globally optimal joint behavior in the studied framework.
icml-2021-fop-factorizing-optimal-joint-.tldr: FOP factorizes a maximum-entropy optimal joint policy into individual policies and proves their convergence to the global optimum.

paragraphs: End-to-end speech translation needs representations that connect spoken input with language expressed in text. The paper argues that learning from only one input modality limits this connection and makes systems overly dependent on scarce parallel speech-translation data. It proposes learning a unified representation from a broader collection of speech and text resources.

Fused Acoustic and Text Masked Language Modeling, or FAT-MLM, jointly learns from acoustic and textual inputs. Its training sources can include paired data for speech recognition, paired data for machine translation, and standalone speech or text. This expands the kinds of corpora that can contribute to representation learning before the translation model is fine-tuned.

The authors then introduce FAT-ST, an end-to-end speech-translation model within the same cross-modal framework. Across three translation directions, fine-tuning from FAT-MLM substantially improves translation quality, with gains reaching 5.9 BLEU. The results support unified acoustic-and-text pretraining as a way to improve speech translation using resources beyond direct speech-translation pairs.
icml-2021-fused-acoustic-and-text-encodi.tldr: Joint speech-and-text pretraining uses diverse corpora to improve end-to-end speech translation by up to 5.9 BLEU.

paragraphs: This paper builds graph neural networks around framelet transforms, which represent graph data at multiple scales. The transform separates the input into low-pass and high-pass coefficients. These components provide the basis for a graph convolution that can work with different frequency content rather than treating the graph representation as a single undivided signal.

The same decomposition also supplies a pooling strategy. It aggregates graph features into low-pass and high-pass spectra while accounting for both feature values and graph geometry, and the paper states that this conserves total information. Networks using the proposed convolution and pooling achieve state-of-the-art results on many node- and graph-prediction tasks.

The authors additionally replace ReLU with shrinkage, an activation that thresholds high-frequency coefficients at different scales. Compared with ReLU, it improves denoising and signal compression: the reported results reduce noise in both nodes and graph structure, and compress signals below half their original size while largely preserving prediction performance. The decomposition thus supports prediction, noise removal, and compression within one framework.
icml-2021-how-framelets-enhance-graph-ne.tldr: Framelet-based graph networks use multiscale frequency representations to improve prediction, denoising, and compression.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search alternates between training network weights and adjusting parameters that describe the architecture. The architecture update needs to account for how weight training affects performance. Computing this architecture gradient, also called a hypergradient, is a key obstacle to scaling the search and finding good designs.

iDARTS uses the implicit function theorem to compute the hypergradient from the obtained solution of the inner weight-training problem. This makes the calculation independent of the optimization path used to reach that solution. The authors then introduce a stochastic approximation to reduce the computational demands of the hypergradient calculation further.

The theoretical result is expected convergence of architecture optimization to a stationary point, which does not imply a globally best architecture. Experiments across two NAS benchmark search spaces and a common NAS search space support the method’s effectiveness. The resulting architectures outperform those found by the baseline methods by large margins, connecting the revised gradient computation to improved search outcomes in the tested settings.
icml-2021-idarts-differentiable-architec.tldr: iDARTS uses stochastic implicit hypergradients to reduce architecture-search computation and improve the architectures found in tested search spaces.

paragraphs: Datasets intended for similar purposes can still describe their examples using incompatible labels. Their annotation sets may not overlap, or one dataset may use broader categories and another finer distinctions. This paper studies how to join such datasets systematically so that neural-network learning can draw on them together.

The central idea is to perform augmentation in label space. The paper contrasts this with joining datasets through latent vectors whose meanings are difficult to interpret. Working with labels brings the category discrepancies into the method itself, making differences in annotation granularity and hierarchy part of the problem being addressed.

The proposed technique combines an artificially constructed knowledge graph, recurrent neural networks, and policy-gradient learning to accomplish label-space dataset joining. Empirical results on both image classification and text classification support the approach’s validity. Its significance is the use of label relationships as the basis for combining datasets, offering a systematic route for connecting resources that serve related purposes but organize their annotations differently.
icml-2021-joining-datasets-via-data-augm.tldr: The method joins related datasets through label-space augmentation that addresses differences in annotation sets, granularity, and hierarchy.

paragraphs: When training labels are corrupted, a noise transition matrix describes how labels from each true class can become other labels. Many methods estimate this matrix through predicted probabilities for the noisy classes. The paper identifies a weakness in that route: neural networks can be overconfident, making those probability estimates unreliable.

The proposed method learns the classifier and the noise transition matrix simultaneously, using only noisy labels. It avoids depending on a separate, error-prone estimate of the noisy class-posterior. Its key ingredient is total variation regularization, motivated by the stochastic label-corruption process and designed to make predicted probability distributions more distinguishable from one another.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove that the transition-matrix estimator is consistent, meaning that its estimate approaches the true matrix as data increases within the analyzed setting. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a different estimation strategy with conditional theoretical support, addressing overconfidence at a step that other approaches rely on.
icml-2021-learning-noise-transition-matr.tldr: Total variation regularization enables joint classifier and label-noise estimation, with consistency of the transition-matrix estimate under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Reasoning over a long sequence becomes costly when a system must keep the entire input available. Memory-augmented networks instead compress the sequence into a bounded memory during one pass and answer later queries from that memory. The paper highlights two problems: early information is gradually forgotten, and useful content is not distinguished from less important content.

Rehearsal Memory addresses both problems through self-supervised rehearsal. Recollection and familiarity tasks train the memory to retain earlier information. A history sampler selects informative fragments for this training, so rehearsal directs attention toward crucial material rather than treating every part of the sequence equally.

The approach connects memory preservation with selective review: the rehearsal tasks target forgetting, while the sampler determines what deserves reinforcement. The authors evaluate it on the synthetic bAbI task and downstream tasks involving text and video question answering and long-sequence recommendation. These evaluations examine the proposed memory mechanism across several uses of stored sequence information; the abstract states the evaluation scope without claiming a particular numerical improvement.
icml-2021-learning-to-rehearse-in-long-s.tldr: Rehearsal Memory uses self-supervised review and selective history sampling to preserve important information from long sequences.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning keeps training data on client devices, but clients still exchange model parameters and update directions such as gradients with a server. Those messages can reveal private information. This paper addresses attacks that infer client information from the learning process even though the original data never leaves the device.

Double-Blind Collaborative Learning, or DBCL, applies random matrix sketching to model weights and generates a fresh sketch at every iteration. From an attacker’s perspective, the sketching acts as random noise strong enough to overwhelm the informative signal. The paper states that this prevents clients from performing gradient-based privacy inference.

The practical aim is to protect these communications without undermining collaborative training. The authors report that DBCL adds little computation or communication cost and does not reduce test accuracy. This addresses the tradeoff they identify in simple defenses, which can fail against attacks or substantially harm accuracy. The stated protection concerns client-side gradient-based inference, keeping the claim tied to the attack mechanism examined.
icml-2021-matrix-sketching-for-secure-co.tldr: DBCL refreshes random sketches of model weights to block client gradient-based privacy inference while reporting little overhead and no accuracy loss.

paragraphs: This paper studies how experience from related estimation tasks can reduce the data needed to identify nonzero entries in a new precision matrix. Each task may have a different matrix and a different pattern of nonzero entries. The central assumption is that the union of these patterns remains small.

The authors pool samples across tasks and fit one matrix using an l1-regularized log-determinant Bregman objective. This is an improper estimate because the tasks do not actually share one true matrix. Nevertheless, with sufficiently many samples, its nonzero pattern recovers the true support union with high probability. For K tasks and N-dimensional data, the sufficient per-task sample complexity scales as O((log N)/K), with a matching lower bound.

For a new task, estimation is then restricted to entries in the learned union. The sufficient sample complexity can fall to O(log(|S_off|)), where |S_off| counts off-diagonal entries in that union. A matching lower bound supports optimality of this scaling. The benefit comes from learning a small set of plausible entries before estimating the new task’s particular pattern.
icml-2021-meta-learning-for-support-reco.tldr: When related precision matrices have a small support union, learning that union reduces the samples sufficient for support recovery in a new task.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning uses experience from previous tasks to adapt quickly to new ones. Sparse rewards make this difficult because an agent must first find experiences that reveal what task it faces. The paper treats this search for informative experience as a learning problem in its own right during both meta-training and adaptation.

MetaCURE separates the exploration policy from the exploitation policy. Its empowerment-driven exploration objective seeks information gain for identifying the task, and the authors derive an intrinsic reward corresponding to that objective. A new off-policy framework learns both policies while allowing them to share knowledge about task inference.

This separation gives exploration a specific purpose: collect information that helps identify the current task, while the exploitation policy learns how to act using that knowledge. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on sparse-reward MuJoCo locomotion tasks and more complex sparse-reward Meta-World tasks. The results support explicitly training task-informative exploration as part of rapid adaptation.
icml-2021-metacure-meta-reinforcement-le.tldr: MetaCURE learns separate exploration and exploitation policies, rewarding exploration that reveals task identity to improve sparse-reward adaptation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples a model-free algorithm needs to learn a policy within epsilon of optimal in a discounted Markov decision process. The analysis tracks the number of states S, actions A, discount factor gamma, desired accuracy epsilon, and allowed failure probability p.

The first algorithm has sample complexity of order SA ln(1/p) divided by epsilon squared and (1−gamma) to the power 5.5, up to polylogarithmic factors. It succeeds with probability at least 1−p. The authors state that this improves on previously known model-free bounds and model-based bounds with tight dependence on the number of states.

For sufficiently small epsilon, a second algorithm improves the exponent on (1−gamma) from 5.5 to 3 while keeping the stated dependence on the other quantities. This bound matches the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. The small-epsilon condition is essential to the stronger result. Together, the guarantees show that model-free learning can attain nearly optimal sample complexity in that regime.
icml-2021-model-free-reinforcement-learn.tldr: The paper gives improved model-free sample-complexity bounds, matching the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors for sufficiently small epsilon.

paragraphs: High-dimensional Bayesian inference requires representing a posterior distribution over many unknown quantities. This can be difficult when the distribution contains several distinct modes. The proposed Multiscale Invertible Generative Network, or MsIGN, uses multiscale structure and the posterior’s low-dimensional nature to make this inference problem more manageable.

MsIGN generates samples from coarse to fine scales. It starts in lower dimensions, then repeatedly upsamples and refines the samples as dimensionality increases. Training also proceeds in stages and minimizes Jeffreys divergence. The paper presents this training objective as a way to avoid mode dropping, where parts of a multimodal posterior are missed.

On two high-dimensional Bayesian inverse problems, MsIGN outperforms previous approaches in posterior approximation and capturing multiple modes. The authors also test natural-image synthesis, reporting better bits-per-dimension than baseline models and interpretable neurons in intermediate layers. These results connect the coarse-to-fine construction to both distribution modeling and preservation of distinct posterior possibilities in the evaluated problems.
icml-2021-multiscale-invertible-generati.tldr: MsIGN generates and refines samples across scales to improve high-dimensional posterior approximation and capture multiple modes.

paragraphs: This paper develops on-policy reinforcement learning for the long-run average reward objective. It begins by asking how much the average reward can change when one policy replaces another. Existing bounds derived for discounted returns become uninformative in this setting, motivating an analysis that addresses average reward directly.

The new bound depends on the average divergence between the policies and on Kemeny’s constant. Using that bound, the authors construct an iterative procedure whose policies improve monotonically under the average-reward criterion. This provides a theoretical basis for policy updates designed around sustained reward rather than an adaptation of an unsuitable discounted-return bound.

The procedure can be combined with established deep reinforcement-learning methods to obtain practical algorithms. The paper develops Average-Reward TRPO, or ATRPO, by adapting TRPO to this objective. Experiments show that ATRPO significantly outperforms TRPO in the most challenging MuJoCo environments considered. The monotonic-improvement result belongs to the theoretical iterative procedure, while the practical algorithm’s advantages are demonstrated empirically.
icml-2021-on-policy-deep-reinforcement-l.tldr: A direct average-reward policy bound supports monotonic policy improvement and motivates ATRPO, which outperforms TRPO in challenging MuJoCo evaluations.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit offers several choices, each producing uncertain outcomes. This paper studies selecting the m choices with the highest values at a specified quantile, using a fixed sampling budget. The motivation is risk-averse decision-making, where a chosen point in an outcome distribution may matter more than its average.

The authors develop asymmetric, two-sided concentration inequalities for order statistics and quantiles. These results apply to random variables with non-decreasing hazard rates. The inequalities control estimation errors on both sides and provide the mathematical basis for analyzing decisions made from a limited number of observations.

Using these bounds, the paper analyzes Q-SAR, a quantile-based version of Successive Accepts and Rejects. It derives an upper bound on the probability of selecting the wrong arms, providing the stated first justification for a quantile-based algorithm for fixed-budget identification of multiple best arms. Illustrative experiments accompany the analysis. The contribution connects a risk-sensitive selection objective with explicit control of identification error under the stated distributional condition.
icml-2021-quantile-bandits-for-best-arms.tldr: Q-SAR identifies multiple high-quantile bandit arms under a fixed budget, with an error-probability bound based on new concentration inequalities.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can defend against perturbed inputs without ensuring equally strong robustness on unseen examples. This paper examines that generalization problem through the network’s latent representations. The authors argue that adversarial perturbations push examples from the same class in different feature-space directions, creating dispersion between training and test adversarial representations.

Their analysis upper-bounds the robust generalization gap using the ordinary generalization gap on natural data plus a term measuring inconsistent feature shifts. This gives the proposed explanation a theoretical connection to robustness: variation in how perturbations move features contributes to the bound, alongside ordinary generalization error.

Shift consistency regularization, or SCR, is designed to reduce that inconsistency during adversarial training. It steers same-class features from natural and adversarial examples toward a common direction. The authors evaluate its effectiveness through extensive comparisons on datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The contribution is a representation-based training intervention motivated by the bound; the analysis offers an upper bound rather than an exact decomposition of observed error.
icml-2021-towards-better-robust-generali.tldr: SCR encourages consistent latent feature shifts during adversarial training to address a theoretically motivated source of poor robust generalization.

paragraphs: Visual event reasoning asks a model to produce cause-and-effect descriptions that extend beyond what a still image directly shows. The descriptions may concern earlier events, the present situation, or what happens afterward. This paper addresses the challenge of connecting information across both spatial relationships and different moments.

Hypergraph-Enhanced Graph Reasoning first represents content within each modality as a semantic graph, allowing it to model relationships inside that modality. Its Graph Self-Attention Enhancement then lets graph representations from different modalities strengthen one another. Multimodal hypergraphs associated with different moments provide additional information to enhance each semantic graph.

The model re-projects these enhanced representations and uses them to generate textual cause-and-effect descriptions. The authors report that the enhancement produces more robust representations than versions without it and that the complete model significantly outperforms compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach matters because it combines within-modality relationships, cross-modality relationships, and information organized across moments in the representation used for event description.
icml-2021-two-heads-are-better-than-one-.tldr: Semantic graphs and multimodal hypergraphs jointly strengthen representations for generating cause-and-effect descriptions beyond a still image.

paragraphs: Planning with a learned world model often means predicting one step after another into the future. Errors can accumulate as the planning horizon grows, causing imagined trajectories to diverge from reality. This paper proposes a graph-based world model that represents sparse, multi-step transitions to support reasoning over longer spans.

The method, L3P, learns latent landmarks as graph nodes. These landmarks are spread across the goal space according to reachability, so their placement reflects how goals can be reached. Graph edges contain reachability estimates distilled from Q-functions. Planning can therefore work with connections between landmarks rather than relying entirely on a long chain of one-step predictions.

Across high-dimensional continuous-control tasks involving robotic manipulation and navigation, L3P significantly outperforms prior work. The authors report that it is often the only evaluated method able to combine model-free reinforcement learning’s robustness with graph search’s generalization. The findings support learned landmark graphs as a promising representation for temporally extended planning in the tested environments.
icml-2021-world-model-as-a-graph-learnin.tldr: L3P learns a graph of latent landmarks and multi-step reachability estimates to improve long-horizon planning in continuous-control tasks.
